segments.narration: It's a June morning in nineteen eighty-five. Katherine Yarbrough — Katie — arrives for a follow-up radiation treatment. She is sixty-one years old, and she knows the procedure. You lie on the table. The technician positions the machine. You hold still. It takes a few seconds. You don't feel much of anything.
segments.visual_description: A lone woman, seen from behind, walks the long empty 1985 hospital corridor toward the distant treatment-room door - small against the receding hallway, routine and unhurried. The camera follows her in one continuous take.

segments.narration: The machine is called the Therac-25. It's the newest of its kind — more compact, more versatile, run entirely by computer. And it is trusted completely. Even when it lies.
segments.visual_description: A treatment room. The Therac-25 machine looming overhead. Oppressive, clinical atmosphere.

segments.narration: The technician enters the prescription. The machine fires. Katie Yarbrough feels something she's never felt before. A tremendous force of heat — a red-hot searing across her shoulder. You burned me, she tells the technician. And the technician tells her that is not possible. Something is wrong. She knows it immediately.
segments.visual_description: An illustrated older woman on the treatment table, a sharp flinch of pain - the moment a routine turns wrong.

segments.narration: She's just received fifteen to twenty thousand rads of radiation. A typical treatment dose is about two hundred.
segments.visual_description: Analog dose meter needle slamming past the danger arc - a dose that should never read this high.

segments.narration: That's up to one hundred times the intended dose. And the machine? It noticed nothing. The console stayed calm. The printer that would have recorded the dose sat disabled. As far as the Therac-25 knew… the treatment had gone exactly to plan.
segments.visual_description: The control terminal serene in the foreground, reporting a normal treatment, while beyond the open doorway behind it the patient on the table flinches under the Therac-25 - the machine's lie and its cost held in one frame.

segments.narration: No alarm. No error. No indication that anything had gone wrong at all. Over the next two years, this machine will overdose six patients in two countries. At least three of them will die of it. The company that built it will insist, again and again, that an overdose is impossible. And the answer will come down to a single byte of memory. How did this happen?
segments.visual_description: The control terminal glowing calm - no alarm, no error, no indication.

segments.narration: The Therac-25 had two ways to fire a beam. One of them could kill. In electron mode, a low-power beam treats the patient directly. In X-ray mode, the beam runs about a hundred times stronger. It fires into a metal target, and the target turns that force into X-rays. The target takes the punishment. The patient gets the treatment. Two modes. One machine. And everything depends on the target being exactly where it's supposed to be.
segments.visual_description: Animated diagram of the Therac-25 linear accelerator. Must show the turntable mechanism with both the target and the scanning magnets. NOT a generic linac.

segments.narration: Previous models — the Therac-6 and the Therac-20 — used hardware safety interlocks. Physical metal. Fuses, switches, mechanical locks that wouldn't let the beam fire unless the target sat in its proper place.
segments.visual_description: Inside an earlier linac chassis: a heavy electromechanical safety interlock — physical metal that made overdose impossible.

segments.narration: The Therac-25's manufacturer — a company called AECL — removed them. It was a deliberate decision: the hardware seemed redundant, an expense the software made unnecessary. AECL trusted its code that much. Nearly every safety check now lived in software alone. Software written in PDP-11 assembly language. By a single programmer. Over several years.
segments.visual_description: A single 1985 terminal alone in the dark, dense amber code scrolling — every safety check now living only in software.

segments.narration: Years before the machine hurt a single patient, AECL ran a safety analysis on the Therac-25. That analysis apparently excluded the software entirely.
segments.visual_description: A thick 1980s safety report under a hard lamp — dense type up top, a conspicuously blank lower band: the analysis never done.

segments.narration: What happened to Katie Yarbrough… happened again. And again. In hospital after hospital, for nearly two years.
segments.visual_description: A records room of identical repeating forms - not an isolated incident.

segments.narration: It starts with Katie Yarbrough, the woman on the table in Georgia. Up to twenty thousand rads, against a typical dose of two hundred. Her hospital's physicist — a man named Tim Still — is the first to ask whether the machine could have burned her. He puts the question to AECL. Three days later, the company's engineers call back: not possible. There's no investigation. Just a phone call.
segments.visual_description: The phone call that closed the case — Tim Still's question to AECL, dismissed as 'not possible,' no investigation.

segments.narration: AECL states that an overdose is impossible.
segments.visual_description: A typewritten institutional denial letter on a bare desk — the corporate claim that an overdose was impossible.

segments.narration: Weeks later, the pattern crosses a border. In Ontario, a forty-year-old woman named Frances Hill goes in for treatment. The machine gives her an estimated thirteen to seventeen thousand rads. Before the year is out, she is dead. Her autopsy notes radiation damage.
segments.visual_description: The aftermath — an empty draped gurney and an open autopsy file under a hard lamp, radiation damage noted; Frances Hill is gone.

segments.narration: By winter it's reached the Pacific Northwest — Yakima, a community hospital among the evergreens. A patient develops striped burns across her hip. Stripes that match the slots of the machine's own hardware. Her hospital writes to AECL and asks the question directly.
segments.visual_description: The stripe signature — a parallel burn pattern that matches the slots of the machine's own collimator hardware.

segments.narration: AECL claims the Therac-25 could not have been responsible for the Yakima injuries.
segments.visual_description: The Yakima hospital, cold and somber - the manufacturer's flat denial.

segments.narration: Three overdoses. Zero acknowledgment.
segments.visual_description: Three unanswered incident folders in a dark office - three overdoses, zero acknowledgment.

segments.narration: Spring comes, and the machines are still treating patients. In an East Texas cancer center, Voyne Ray Cox lies on the table for his ninth treatment. The operator knows her console. She's fast. She types an X where she meant an E. Catches it. Cursors up. Fixes it. The beam fires — and in the treatment room, Cox feels a jolt like an electric shock. She can't see him. The video monitor to his room is dead, and the intercom's broken. All she sees is her screen: Malfunction fifty-four. A code no manual explains. And the dose reading shows next to nothing — an underdose. Stops like this happen all the time, and the procedure for them is simple. Her finger moves to the P key.
segments.visual_description: The Tyler control room, sealed off from the treatment room: the operator works fast at her console, a typo caught and corrected, while the video monitor to Cox's room sits dead beside her screen - then the error code and a low dose reading, and her finger moving to the P key.

segments.narration: The operator presses P… The machine fires a second time. Cox is getting off the table when it hits him. He pounds on the treatment room door. Simulations will later put the doses at sixteen to twenty-five thousand rads. Delivered in under a second. Into an area about one centimeter across.
segments.visual_description: Inside the sealed treatment room — the beam fires a second time and the patient, a lone silhouette, pounds on the unanswered door.

segments.narration: Twenty-five thousand rads. One second. One centimeter.
segments.visual_description: The terminal calm as an invisible catastrophe lands - the dose, the second, the centimeter.

segments.narration: Three weeks later. Same hospital. Same machine. Same operator. Verdon Kidd is on the table, receiving treatment to his face. Another overdose. This time the hospital physicist, Fritz Hager, begins his own investigation. He will eventually reproduce the error himself.
segments.visual_description: Tyler treatment room again, a new patient - the machine head swinging down over him.

segments.narration: Verdon Kidd is dead within twenty days — what one researcher will later call the first death of its kind. Voyne Ray Cox dies five months after his accident. Katie Yarbrough survives. The radiation takes her breast, and the use of her arm and shoulder. The pain never leaves.
segments.visual_description: A hushed empty hall, cold light and drifting dust - a memorial to the dead.

segments.narration: For months — nothing. Long enough to believe it's over. In the dead of winter, nineteen eighty-seven, it returns to Yakima — the same hospital from before. Sixty-five-year-old Glen Dodd takes eight to ten thousand rads. His prescribed dose was eighty-six. By spring, he, too, is dead.
segments.visual_description: Yakima again, deep winter - a lone mourner; the pattern returning.

segments.narration: Six known accidents. At least three dead. Spanning nearly two years. And the manufacturer called an overdose impossible — until the same machine, in the same room, did it again.
segments.visual_description: The terminal glowing calm amber as identical printouts pile up beside it — harm accumulating, the machine unbothered.

segments.narration: In Tyler, Fritz Hager doesn't let it go. After hours, he sits at the machine with the operator, and she re-types her exact keystrokes. Again. And again. It takes practice — but then it comes: Malfunction fifty-four, on demand. Speed is the trigger. AECL's engineers can't reproduce it… until they're told to type fast. Then they find it, buried in the code. And it isn't alone. The software carries two bugs.
segments.visual_description: After hours in the Tyler control room: the operator re-types her exact keystrokes at the terminal while the hospital physicist watches over her shoulder - hunting the error until Malfunction 54 appears on demand.

segments.narration: The first was a race condition. Setting up the beam takes the machine about eight seconds. And the screen lets an operator keep typing while it works. Type X-ray by mistake. Catch it. Cursor up, fix it to electron — all inside those eight seconds. The screen takes the correction. The turntable follows it. But the beam setting never hears about the change… It stays locked at X-ray strength. A hundred times the current of an electron treatment.
segments.visual_description: Race condition animation — two parallel timelines: 'Software state' and 'Hardware state' diverging. Software shows one mode, hardware stays in another.

segments.narration: The machine fires the full-power beam with no target and no flattening filter. Directly into the patient. And the chambers that measure dose can't keep up. They saturate — and report almost nothing. The machine doesn't even know what it's done.
segments.visual_description: Animation shows beam firing unimpeded — the moment of catastrophic failure. Hard visual impact.

segments.narration: The second bug was an arithmetic overflow. Deep in the setup routine, the software tracked one safety check with a counter called Class Three. The counter was a single byte. One byte. A maximum value of two hundred and fifty-five. Every pass of the routine pushed it up by one. And at two hundred and fifty-five, the next push didn't raise an error. It rolled over… to zero.
segments.visual_description: Byte overflow animation — a single byte counter incrementing: 253, 254, 255... then rolling to 0. The moment the safety check vanishes.

segments.narration: Zero. The value that told the software: nothing needs checking. For that one pass in every two hundred and fifty-six, the turntable check simply vanished. If the operator pressed the set button at that exact moment… the software saw no reason to stop. The interlocks were satisfied. The beam fired — turntable out of position, target out of the path. That is the bug that came back for Yakima, in the dead of winter. For Glen Dodd. And there was no hardware interlock left to catch it. AECL had removed them.
segments.visual_description: Counter reads 0. Green 'SAFE' indicator illuminates. Beam fires. The false safety signal.

segments.narration: The same race condition lived in the older Therac-20 — for years. At a teaching clinic in Chicago, students' creative edits kept tripping breakers and blowing fuses. A nuisance. It never hurt anyone. The hardware caught what the software missed. The Therac-25 had no fuses left to blow.
segments.visual_description: The machine armed in the dark, one amber lamp lit - every safeguard stripped away.

segments.narration: Both bugs had been there all along. Hiding in the code, waiting — for an operator to type fast enough, for a counter to land on zero. The race condition was older than the Therac-25 itself: carried in, line by line, from machines a decade before. And every time the screen said Malfunction fifty-four, operators pressed P. They proceeded. Because no manual explained it. Because stops like it were everyday noise — one clinic logged forty in a single day. Because the machine itself had trained them to ignore it.
segments.visual_description: MALFUNCTION 54 surfacing again and again — a warning seen so often it has stopped meaning anything.

segments.narration: One day after Verdon Kidd's death, the FDA declared the Therac-25 defective and demanded a corrective action plan. It took five revisions. AECL took another fourteen months to deliver the final version — more than two years after the machine burned Katie Yarbrough. More than twenty-three changes. And among them, the one that mattered most: they put back the very safeguard they'd removed to build it.
segments.visual_description: An FDA letter, federal seal embossed - the regulatory response landing.

segments.narration: Even before the plan was final, the FDA recommended pulling every Therac-25 out of service. In an internal memo, the agency admitted it could never find every failure mode hiding in the software. Within a few years, AECL was out of the medical machine business entirely.
segments.visual_description: The terminal's glow dims and dies — units removed from service, the screen going dark for good.

segments.narration: Researchers Nancy Leveson and Clark Turner published the definitive investigation of the Therac-25 accidents. It became a standard case study in software engineering — taught to this day. Because the bugs were ordinary. The failures around them were human. Thirty years on, Leveson returned to it with a warning: these accidents were simply the first of many.
segments.visual_description: The Leveson & Turner academic paper under a lamp - a hand studying the document.

segments.narration: Overconfidence in software. Removal of redundant safety systems. A manufacturer that called overdoses impossible while patients were dying. Operators trained by the machine itself to ignore its warnings. And a safety analysis that never analyzed the software at all.
segments.visual_description: Empty treatment room, machine powered down, the light fading - the machine at rest.

segments.narration: The Therac-25 didn't fail because the technology was too complex. It failed because the people who built it believed it was too reliable to fail.
segments.visual_description: Dark empty room, the machine a dissolving silhouette - final silence.
